title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
claim: On CRT tasks, correct answers were 5% for GPT-3-davinci-003, 59% for ChatGPT-3.5 and 96% for ChatGPT-4; trap (intuitive) answers were 80%, 15% and 0%; humans 38% correct and 55% trap.
quote: The fraction of correct responses equaled 59% for ChatGPT-3.5 and 96% for ChatGPT-4.
n: CRT tasks, human and LLM comparison
transfer: Model strength decides whether the first natural answer is a trap. A small model may need the doubt step; a strong one may not. Measure trap rate per model before gating.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
claim: Telling davinci-003 to use algebra (chain of thought) cut trap answers from 80% to 29% and raised correct from 5% to 28%, but atypical wrong answers rose from 15% to 43%.
quote: significantly reduced a model's tendency to fall for the trap embedded in the task, as illustrated by the drop in the fraction of intuitive responses from 80% to 29%
transfer: Forced reasoning removes traps in weak models but adds new errors. Pair it with a checker.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
claim: Forbidding chain of thought left ChatGPT-3.5 correct rate unchanged and cut ChatGPT-4 from 95% to 88%: strong chat models solve most CRT items without visible reasoning.
quote: The fraction of correct responses for ChatGPT-3.5 did not significantly change
transfer: For strong models, extra deliberation on trap puzzles gives a small gain at most. Supports gating doubt.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
claim: Semantic illusions: correct answers 18% for davinci-003, 74% ChatGPT-3.5, 88% ChatGPT-4; davinci fell for the illusion 72% of the time.
quote: The fraction of correct responses increased from 18% for GPT-3-davinci-003 to 74% and 88% for ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4

authors: Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, Le, Chi, Narang, Chowdhery, Zhou
title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
claim: Self-consistency paper: agreement among sampled paths (share of decodes matching the final answer) is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K for PaLM-540B.
quote: the consistency (in terms of % of decodes agreeing with the final aggregated answer) is highly correlated with accuracy
transfer: Agreement is a usable confidence signal in-distribution. Use it as a router input, but remember correlated errors (Kim 2025).

title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
venue: arXiv:2304.05128 (abstract page; quote is from fetched summary, wording not exact)
claim: Self-debugging: letting the model see execution results of its own code raised accuracy by 2-3% on Spider without unit tests, and by up to 12% on TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests; it matched baselines using over 10x more samples.
quote: Self-Debugging with code explanation consistently improves the baseline by 2-3%
transfer: Run the code and feed back the result. Gains are larger when real tests exist. Abstract only, no self-critique-only arm read.

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
claim: Language models can estimate P(True) for their own proposed answers; larger models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false questions, and self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples first.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions
transfer: Showing the model several candidates before judging one is a cheap agreement-like signal. Calibration is format-dependent.

CHECK: counterexample search or mental model prompting improves LLM syllogism or rule induction (mReasoner, Johnson-Laird, Khemlani). VERDICT: UNRESOLVED. No paper found; a guessed arXiv id turned out to be an unrelated paper and was discarded. The gap in the critique stays open.

CHECK: Does agreement predict correctness? VERDICT: PARTLY SETTLED. Wang 2023 shows a strong correlation on GSM8K (d-06), and Kadavath 2022 shows self-evaluation over samples helps (d-08). Both use one model on mostly in-distribution tasks. They do not contradict Kim 2025 (60% shared wrong answers): agreement ranks items well on average yet can be confidently wrong when errors are shared. No AUROC table was opened. Use agreement as a soft router input, never as proof.

CHECK: Does execution beat self-critique? VERDICT: PARTLY SETTLED. Self-Debug (d-07) gains from execution feedback, with larger gains when tests exist, consistent with Stechly and Huang already in the set. No paper opened that compares both arms head to head, so the size of the gap is unmeasured here.
